question.text: Although not a province, this Canadian territory is the newest, having been created in 1999 as a territory for the Inuit peoples.
question.clue: In 1999, this large territory became a separate territory from the Northwest Territories.

swap.leadin: Answer these questions about English monarchs.
swap.text: George V and Elizabeth II are of this ruling house.
swap.clue: Considered one of the automotive capitals of Canada, this city lies at one end of the Ambassador Bridge across the Detroit River from Detroit.

question.leadin: Phrases like "sick animal," "trained seal," "evil genius," "does not have a spine," and "devoid of honour" are listed as unparliamentary language in a book titled for Arthur Beauchesne, a clerk of this body.
question.text: Name this lower house of Canadian Parliament, which shares its name with the house in the UK contrasted with the House of Lords.
question.clue: The ability of wealthy men to purchase housing and instill tenants willing to vote as they wished, along with the outsized representation possible in districts with a tiny number of residents, led to reform of this body in 1832.

swap.leadin: Louis Riel led an uprising of these people in the Red River Colony.
swap.text: Name these people, who were mixed-race descendants of aboriginal Canadians and European Settlers.
swap.clue: Garnet Wolseley led a namesake expedition to confront these people in 1870.

question.text: Chretien was a member of this center-left Canadian political party which often competes with the Conservative Party.
question.clue: A request to dissolve parliament by a leader of this party was refused by Governor-General Julian Byng in 1926.

swap.text: This British General, the victor at the Battle of the Plains of Abraham, was killed during the course of battle. He served as Henry Hawley's aide-de-camp during the Jacobite Rebellion.
swap.clue: He served as quartermaster during an attack on Rochefort in which he was unable to convince John Mordaunt to execute a frontal assault.

question.leadin: Answer the following about the wildly unpopular acts passed by Parliament in the lead-up to the American Revolution.
question.text: This law, passed in 1774 among the "intolerable acts," expanded its namesake region into the modern-day Midwest and controversially allowed Catholicism to be practiced there.
question.clue: This 1774 act allowed the free practice of Catholicism in its namesake colony, and also defined the boundary for that colony.

swap.leadin: Invading Canada never seems to go well for the United States.
swap.text: Name this first defeat of the Continental Army during the American Revolutionary War. This battle was named after the namesake-city of this French-speaking province.
swap.clue: This battle immediately followed an engagement at Beauport, and this battle was precipitated by a nighttime trip to the landing point past the Montmorency River at Anse de Foulon.

question.leadin: Answer the following about the Manitoba schools question of the 1890s.
question.text: The Manitoba Schools Question allowed this man to defeat Charles Tupper in the 1896 federal election. This man was Canada's first French-speaking prime minister.
question.clue: This replacement of Charles Tupper created his nation's "tin pot" navy when he signed the Naval Service Bill.

swap.leadin: Name some important events involving the Quebec sovereignty movement.
swap.text: This agreement, which was not ratified due to the opposition of Manitoba and Newfoundland, declared that Quebec was a "distinct society." It was the catalyst for the creation of the Bloc Quebecois (BLOK ke-bec-WA).
swap.clue: The inventor Thomas "Carbide" Wilson, who patented a process for calcium carbide, owned the summer house where this document was created.

question.leadin: In 1970 the members of the terrorist group FLQ kidnapped two officials in Canada.
question.text: Name this situation named for the month it took place.
question.clue: Robert Bourassa appeared on television five minutes prior to a deadline in this event stating that his government would not negotiate, resulting in the retaliatory execution of Pierre LaPorte, who had been kidnapped along with James Cross.

swap.text: While he was PM of Canada during the October Crisis in 1970, Pierre Trudeau famously responded to a question about how far he'd go in the suspension of civil liberties with this three-word phrase.
swap.clue: When asked by journalist Tim Ralfe how far he would go to resolve the October Crisis, Trudeau famously gave this three-word response.

question.leadin: This organization kidnapped James Cross and killed Pierre Laporte.
question.text: Name this organization whose actions led to the October Crisis.
question.answerHtml: Front de libération du Québec (or FLQ, or Felquistes, or Quebec Liberation Front)
question.clue: Members of this group kidnapped British Trade Commissioner James Cross and Minister of Labour and Immigration Pierre Laporte.

swap.text: This world leader accepted American Bomarc missiles onto his country's soil but only equipped with conventional warheads. He also controversially scrapped the Avro Arrow program.
swap.clue: He also cancelled the Avro Arrow program, halting production of fighter jets in his country, when he signed NORAD with the US. Raised in Saskatchewan, he passed his country's Bill of Rights, and presided over the opening of the St. Lawrence Seaway.

question.text: Earlier PC premier Bill Davis extended funding to Ontario high schools of this kind often used by Franco-Ontarians. After the Manitoba Schools Question, schools operated by this kind of system were re-established without funding by Prime Minister Wilfried Laurier.
question.answerHtml: Catholic schools [prompt on religious schools; prompt on answers involving the use of French by asking “what other quality did those schools have?”]

swap.leadin: Answer these questions about an occasion of fraternity and goodwill, the first Thanksgiving.
swap.text: The Pilgrims were actually scooped by Canadian Thanksgiving, which may have begun when this founder of Quebec shared a meal with natives as part of the Order of Good Cheer - a group of his most prolific Indian-killers. He names a lake on the border of Quebec and Vermont.
swap.clue: At the Battle of Sorel during the Beaver Wars, he allied with the Algonquin and Huron tribes to defeat the Iroquois.

question.text: This woman is known as the Canadian Paul Revere for walking over twenty miles to warn the British of an attack, which directly led to the American loss at the Battle of Beaver Dams.

swap.leadin: Zachariah Gilliam's correspondence with these people led to the foundation of the then-largest corporation based in the Western Hemisphere.
swap.text: Name these First Nations peoples whose various chiefs included Poundmaker and Big Bear. Along with the Stoney, they were the largest by population within the Iron Confederacy.

question.leadin: This man passed the Padlock Act to allow the closing of buildings used to propagate "communism," and was slapped with a fine for revoking Frank Roncarelli's liquor license in a landmark supreme court case.
question.text: Name this leader nicknamed "le Chef," whose government also certified around 20,000 healthy orphans as mentally ill and shipped them to asylums in order to receive federal subsidies.
question.clue: This Quebecois leader who implemented a set of conservative policies called the Great Darkness before his Union Nationale Party was deposed in 1959.

swap.leadin: A group devoted to this cause abducted and killed Pierre Laporte in the October Crisis.
swap.text: Name this political objective that was narrowly rejected by voters in a 1995 referendum during the Mulroney government.
swap.answerHtml: Quebec independence [accept word forms but require both Quebec and independence; accept sovereignty for “independence”]
swap.clue: The Quiet Revolution led to it becoming an issue of national importance.
